utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again, you are being reminded that you are bound by the declaration you took to tell the truth, nothing else but the truth. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Before I resume my questions, and I think today will be my last day of questions for Mr. Babic, the issue with respect to the 89(F) statement has been resolved. It can be admitted into evidence as it was submitted to the court and I believe the Registrar has set aside numbers for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the 89(F) notice please be admitted into evidence, and may it please be given exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibits 135 through Exhibit 172, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Maybe before we begin can I just sort of hand down the decision on cross-examination. The Trial Chamber is seized of the Prosecution motion for an order regarding cross-examination filed on the 2nd of February in which the Prosecution requested that the Trial Chamber rule on three matters as follows. One, that the cross-examining party should provide to the opposing party no later than the commencement of the cross-examination, a list of those documents or exhibits which it intends to use during the cross-examination of a witness. Two, that the cross-examining party should not, however, generally be prohibited from using other documents not provided or included in the list. And three, that if it appears that the cross-examining party has omitted a document for the sole purpose of obtaining unfair surprise or for another improper purpose the Trial Chamber may grant an opposing party a recess for adjournment or it may preclude the use of the document during the cross-examination. The Trial Chamber notes that the Defence in its response filed on the 15th of February 2006 has agreed with points 1 and 2 of the proposed procedure but disputes point 3. The Prosecution in its reply on the 17th of February 2006 is prepared to abandon point 3, to be considered in the future as and when the need arises. Considering the above positions of the parties, the Trial Chamber grants the motion only with respect to points 1 and 2, and point 3 is denied. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: May I proceed? Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Babic. Are you able to understand me clearly in your language?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As always, if you cannot understand me in your language or you don't understand my question, please tell me. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you now about -- we are up to the fall of 1991, August/September 1991 and I would like to talk to you now about various armed forces that were operating in different areas of the SAO Krajina during the fall of 1991, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And for the assistance of the Trial Chamber it might be useful to have at the ready map 3 of Exhibit 22, because there will be a number of references to municipalities, and just for ease of following the evidence, that might be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I want to focus first on the northern part of the SAO Krajina. That is from, say, Korenica to Kostajnica. And I want to focus first on which JNA units were operating in that area during the fall of 1991. And that area is basically Kordun and Banija and Korenica is obviously in Lika. So could you tell us first what you know about which JNA units were operating in that northern part of the SAO Krajina during the fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That area fell under the 5th army district of the JNA, that had its command in Zagreb. In that area, there was the Zagreb corps, and the Rijeka corps, as well as the units that operated in the area of Krajina, beginning with the JNA garrison of Petrinja, the artillery drill ground in Slunj, the JNA division command in Gospic, and parts of the air corps, together with the airfield in Bihac, covering parts of the territory that included Korenica in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who was the commander of the 5th army district of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Andrija Raseta. I'm not sure whether he was the actual commander or deputy commander of the 5th army district, that is the Zagreb army district, but I know he was the most superior officer in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You referred to the Zagreb corps and the Rijeka corps. Do you know who the commander of those -- who the commanders of those corps were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Nikola Uzelac was commander of the Zagreb corps but I don't know who was the commander of the Rijeka corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Nikola Uzelac was from where, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nikola Uzelac was a native of Lika. He was from Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, do you know what -- what happened, if anything, to non-Serb generals who were in the JNA during 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the war in 1991, lots of generals and high-ranking officers of non-Serb ethnicity were replaced. What I know about is the Rijeka corps, and its territory, and I also heard about what happened in other areas but my specific knowledge is about that particular territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: JNA unit commanders, including the corps commander, Chief of Staff, chief of artillery in the Knin corps who were Macedonians, Slovenes, et cetera, were replaced by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Just to be clear on the record here because initially what we got in your answer was that you knew about the Rijeka corps and its territory, and then in answer to my last question you spoke about the Knin corps. So was it the Knin corps or the Rijeka corps that you knew about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knin corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, just going back to the JNA formations that were in the northern part of the SAO Krajina, you referred to garrisons at Petrinja and Slunj. Was there a garrison also in Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one in Karlovac, and also one in an area called encampment, where armoured artillery units were based, but that is just on the border of the area of SAO Krajina, around Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is that area called again?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They referred to it as Logoriste, which means encampment. Whether it's an official name or whether it was a local name given it by the people, but those were the barracks and facilities of the JNA south of Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the garrison at Slunj was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All I know is that later on, when fighting had already started to liberate Slunj, Colonel Cedo Bulat appeared. I don't know whether he had been in the area of Slunj before or not. He commanded the 5th Partizan Brigade in the fighting around Slunj and Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was the result of that fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The result was the conquest of the area north of Plitvice, around the drill ground, Slunj municipality, together with the expulsion of the Croat civilians from that area and Serb takeover.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you also mentioned garrisons at Petrinja. Do you know who the commander there was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Slobodan Tarbuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was there anything -- any unit or command located in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Plitvice, there was the outpost of the command of the Rijeka corps, the command of the 6th Lika division, during the fighting, at least. There were also some units from other parts of Yugoslavia and Serbia including the special airborne unit from Nis in the area between Plitvice and Korenica whereas in the north towards Banija and Kordun, there were units from Serbia called the Sabac Brigade, the Vojvodina Brigade, the Loznica Brigade. Those were at least the popular names for those units that had been mobilised in Serbia and brought over to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's talk now about the southern part of the SAO Krajina, essentially what you've identified as Northern Dalmatia. Which units of the JNA operated there? Starting at the corps level.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th Knin corps of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know which -- Mr. Babic, do you know which army or military district the 9th Corps fell under? Or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It belonged to the military naval district that had its command in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the naval military district was at that time, in the fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Admiral Mile Klandic -- Kandic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've spoken earlier in your testimony about the 9th Knin corps but could you tell us again who the commanders of the 9th Corps were in the spring of -- spring, summer, fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May the corps commander was General Trajcevski, an ethnic Macedonian. In the summer, General Trajcevski was replaced by General Spiro Nikovic. In September, General Nikovic was replaced as commander of the 9th Corps by General Vlado Vukovic, and he remained in that command post until the end of the autumn, maybe November or December, 1990, when he was replaced by General Ratko Mladic as commander of the 9th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The translation that we got said that General Ratko Mladic became the commander of the 9th Corps in November or December of 1990. Is it 1990 or 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what happened to General Spiro Nikovic after he left the command in September of 1991? Where did he go, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. He went for a while for two or three weeks maybe, to the General Staff of the JNA in Belgrade, and after that, he got a transfer in early December 1991, and became commander of the 2nd Operational Zone of the JNA in Samarica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was in December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask you some questions about the 2nd Operational Zone of the JNA in a moment. But I want to ask is you some questions now about General Vukovic. Do you know, once he became commander of the 9th Knin corps, do you know who he reported to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He became commander in mid-September 1991, and he was answerable to the General Staff of the JNA, to the chief of the General Staff actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from three different sources. First of all, when he arrived, he said he had received command duty at the General Staff from the federal secretary for National Defence, General Kadijevic, and this transition of duty was done so urgently he hadn't even had time to put on his ceremonial uniform for the occasion. Second, I had information from the chief of the TO, General Kasum that operations in the zone of the 2nd Corps were being conducted from the General Staff in Belgrade, when Chief of the General Staff was General Batic [phoen], and my third source of that information was General Ratko Mladic. He played to me a tape of his conversation with General Adzic which means that he received orders and had direct communication with the General Staff in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I'm going to ask you some questions about that third point in a moment, about the tape played for you by General Mladic but first I just want to clear something up here. General Kasum told you that operations in which zone were being conducted from the General Staff in Belgrade? What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the front line, on the battlefield. He was Chief of Staff for the SAO Krajina and he said literally that not a single tank could be moved on the battlefield unless its position had prior to that been established at the operations centre of the General Staff in Belgrade, as far as the Croatian theatre of war was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you tell us now what were the circumstances of General Ratko Mladic playing a tape for you of a conversation that he had with General Adzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General Mladic invited me to the office of the 9th Corps commander in Knin, and he told me that he, together with a group of officers, had taken the Maslenica bridge without the knowledge of the commanders, the chief of the General Staff and General Spiro Nikovic. He said he had received a call from chief of the General Staff, General Adzic, directly, to criticise him for taking that action without consulting the command. And Mladic said that this operation, the takeover of the Maslenica bridge, was actually done without the knowledge of General Nikovic but they had informed the General Staff otherwise. After that, Adzic talked to Mladic on the phone and Mladic recorded that conversation and played the tape for me. In that telephone call, General Adzic reprimanded Mladic for doing that, and he said that their comrades were under siege in JNA garrisons and barracks in various places. Mladic played this tape for me and asked me if I had any information about this from my political sources, political channels, and that's the reason why he played the tape for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you have any information about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did this episode that you've just described have any consequence for General Nikovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I learned that from Mladic, or as I learned it from Mladic, the General Staff punished General Nikovic in a way by transferring him to the General Staff in Belgrade, placing him in one of the administrations, and after that, the commander of the Knin corps was replaced and General Vukovic was appointed instead. There was a period of about several days during this transition when General Mladic had actual command over the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you made reference earlier to the 6th Lika Division which was operating in Plitvice. Did that -- do you know if that came under the command of the 9th Corps? Or was that under a different command? Or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not fall under the command of the 9th Corps. It belonged to the group of units whose command was located at Plitvice lakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you about different TO units operating in various areas of the SAO Krajina during the fall of 1991. And you've -- you told us earlier that you issued some orders regarding the structuring of the TO at that time. If we could look at 65 ter Exhibit 122, please. Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a document prescribing the formations of the Territorial Defence Staffs of the municipalities of the SAO Krajina. I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour? And just for the record the date of the document is June 21st, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 216, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look now please at 65 ter Exhibit 117?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document? And if the usher could scroll down, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is the order to establish the operative zones of the TO. I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the date of the document is 20th of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 217, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if the usher could just scroll down just a bit, sorry, scroll up so that point 1 is there, perfect. Now, in point 1 there is reference to the 1st operative zone which includes Dalmatia and Lika and it lists various municipalities. Who commanded this zone of the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff in Knin, the commander of the staff in Knin or, rather, General Ilija Djuic from the moment when the staff was formed, from the 30th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, point -- section 2 and 3 of this document talk about the 2nd Operative Zone in Kordun and lists the municipalities and point 3 is the 3rd Operative Zone in Banija and lists the municipalities. Who commanded these zones?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while the commander of the 2nd zone for Kordun was Mile Dakic, commander of the 3rd zone was Dr. Jovic. Those zones were later on turned into a single zone that was commanded by Colonel Vujaklija, from the 30th of September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit 157, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the order for the 2nd and 3rd zone of the Territorial Defence SAO Krajina, Kordun and Banija, a single Territorial Defence Staff is being established. And I signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the date of this document is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30th of September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 218, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter Exhibit number 157 -- 58, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the appointment of Rade Vujaklija, Colonel Vujaklija, as commander of the 2nd and 3rd Operational Zones for Kordun and Banija dated the 30th of September 1991. This is a document that I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will two -- Exhibit number 219, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, was the appointment of Colonel Vujaklija on your initiative or on the initiative of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the initiative of the JNA, it was sent from the General Staff to Kordun. He was there for a while and then he came to see me so that I would write out his appointment on the basis of the regulations of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when he assumed command of the 2nd and 3rd zones, which have been merged, of the TO, who was he subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was subordinated to General Spiro Nikovic, commander of the 2nd Operational Group of the JNA at Samarica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit 164, please? And could we scroll down so the witness can read some of the document, please? There.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a piece of information sent to the Territorial Defence Staffs and municipal Secretariats for National Defence of Gracac, Donji Lapac, and Korenica from the month of October, the 10th of October 1991. I issued this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we just scroll up to the top of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The 5th of October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then could we scroll down so the first paragraph is visible it says at the beginning of first paragraph, "According to our information, in your municipalities, there exists a manifest initiative to form separate operation zones of the Territorial Defence for your three municipalities." Can you explain the circumstances of why you issued this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two types of information that I received from these municipalities or rather two pieces of information that I received from these municipalities, that there were tendencies for this zone to separate itself from Dalmatia and Lika, that zone, and to establish itself as a zone in its own right. A group of generals called for this, JNA generals, who hailed from Lika and who were in Belgrade and people from the 6th Lika Division, and they wanted to have control over all the armed forces in Lika, including the Territorial Defence. That's what it was all about. That's what General Simovic said to me and he gave me some other information too. The second request was from the municipalities, especially Korenica and Lapac. The leaderships of the municipalities that were under the influence of the police or rather the paramilitary structures, and they didn't want to subordinate themselves to Knin. It was their initiative, the reason for the establishment of the zone. That is why this instruction was sent to the municipalities by myself, that the zone remain one, the Dalmatia-Lika zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, just so we are clear on this issue, who, if you know, was trying to establish a separate zone in this area, in Donja Lapac, Korenica and Gracac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I spoke about the generals from Lika who lived in Belgrade, and who had this initiative to establish the 6th Lika Division of the JNA and to send to this division volunteers from Serbia. So they were its proponents. They were retired generals and general who is were still in active service in the JNA. I don't know exactly. They were the participants in this endeavour. That was one line. The second line was protests in the municipalities of Lapac and Korenica. They somehow always believed that the headquarters in Knin or rather the political leadership of these municipalities Rastelica [phoen] and Bozenica [phoen] and the people around them, that the staff in Knin was not under their influence and they always tried to get away from that influence, to get out of the command of that staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With respect to that second point, tell me precisely who is "they" that was trying to get away from the staff of Knin? You mentioned a couple of names but could you elaborate on that a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the president of the municipality of Donji Lapac and there was Bosko Bozanic too. On the 29th of May, after the government was established, they belonged to a group, a political organisational military group in Martic's environment. They were Martic's group that was in opposition to the government at that time. That was their position, and that is the reason why they had this kind of initiatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were they part of the parallel structure that you have described earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, what was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if I put this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 5th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For the 5th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't remember you doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The Registrar will -- if I haven't done it, could it be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is then admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 220, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, what was the first TO Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st TO Brigade was the 1st Partizan Brigade of the JNA that had a dual name. It was the 1st Partizan Brigade of the JNA, that is to say the first light brigade that was established in the territory of the municipality of Gracac but at the same time, it was referred to as the 1st Brigade of the Territorial Defence because that was the way in which the mobilisation of the 1st Partizan Brigade could be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this brigade was subordinated to whom? Or to which structure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the 9th Corps in Knin, the JNA Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who commanded it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Petar Trbovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified a few moments ago that General Spiro Nikovic became commander of the 2nd Operational Group of the JNA. Can you tell me what that was and what area it covered?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Operational Group of the JNA was the operational group of JNA units and Territorial Defence units that covered the area of Kordun and Banija, and part of Lika, around lake Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or, rather, the municipality of Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which units of the JNA and the Territorial Defence were included within this operational group?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units of the Petrinja garrison of the JNA, units that came from Serbia, units that were in the territory of the municipality of Slunj, that is to say a group of units in the area of Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are those units that -- are those TO units or JNA units at the end of your answer there, that were from the territory of Slunj and the units from the area of Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: TO units from the area of Slunj belonged to the command of the 2nd Operational Group, that is to say TO units from the entire area of Kordun and Banija and JNA units from the area of Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were there any police units, to your knowledge, that worked with this structure, the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area, there were police units but they were not subordinated to that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were the police units from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were regular police from the municipalities and there were special units of the police of Krajina stationed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know who commanded those police units in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know part of it. Commander of the special police was Stevo Borojevic in the area of Kostajnica and Samarica. And I don't know exactly who it was in Korenica. I know that Frenki had his headquarters in Korenica at the time, but they had separate units any way. There was the unit of Captain Dragan, the former Knindza that was subordinated to Frenki. I don't know exactly in which area that unit operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where was the headquarters of this operational group?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the hill of Samarica, between Kostajnica and Dvor Na Uni and Samarica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the 7th Banija Division?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 7th Banija Division was a volunteer structure that was established by the parallel government structure in the beginning of the summer of 1991. It was the biggest volunteer unit formed in the territory of the SAO Krajina under the control of the parallel structures. I already spoke about that. This is the unit that was armed by Radmilo Bogdanovic and they were organised in that area. That structure waged war in Dvor Na Uni and Kostajnica, and then under the influence of Mr. Martic, while he was in charge of the Territorial Defence, it was transformed into the Territorial Defence units of Dvor Na Uni and Kostajnica. For a long time, this unit was not subordinated to the command of the operational zone or rather the commander of the operational zone of Territorial Defence for Banija. It was subordinated only from the month of October 1991, as units of Territorial Defence of Dvor and Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And from October of 1991, when it was -- became units of the Territorial Defence of Dvor and Kostajnica, did it have any relation to the 2nd Operative Group or 2nd Operations Group that you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were subordinated to the command of the 2nd Operations Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who was the commander, if you know, of the 7th Banija Division?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogdan Vajagic was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who was this division subordinated to before October 1991, when it was running as a parallel structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During the summer or fall of 1991, did Vojislav Seselj come to the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The end of 1991, he was there in May as well, May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And for what purpose, if you know, did he come to the SAO Krajina on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of 1991, he came to visit his volunteers, who were on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did his volunteers have a name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were individuals in JNA units at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how did he -- how did he get to his volunteers? Was his trip facilitated by anybody?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came with a support of the JNA and the Minister of Defence of Serbia, the minister who replaced General Simovic. I cannot remember his name right now. This was in 1991, Marko Negovanovic was the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seselj told me, Seselj himself told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've made reference to the 6th Lika Division but I don't think I asked you who commanded that division, if you know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I heard, Savo Jurasovic. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it was headquartered where?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to talk to you now, Mr. Babic, about fighting that occurred in various areas in the SAO Krajina during the fall of 1991. And I want to start first with the Kostajnica region, specifically Dubica, Civljani, and Bacin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Your Honours that area in addition to being on map 3 in the Kostajnica area, it's also on page 21 of the atlas that is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you know when fighting started in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It started in the summer of 1991, towards the end of the month of June 1991. That's when fighting started in the area of Banija. In the area of Kostajnica, there was intensive fighting during August and September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know which units were involved in the fighting in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already mentioned, first of all it was the units of the 7th Banija Division, later the units of the Territorial Defence of the police of Krajina, and units of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know how long the fighting lasted in this area, until when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a long time, for a few months, until the beginning of October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In 1991, did you have occasion to go through Kostajnica, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Areas that were populated by Croats were destroyed, and there were no Croats left there. They had either fled or were expelled or moved out after the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to go specifically through Dubica during 1993? Or around then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember which year it was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I passed there in 1993, towards the end of 1993, during the election campaign in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you see in Dubica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many of the settlements where Croats lived were destroyed and there were no Croats left there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were there any Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you later hear anything about what had happened in Dubica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard in 1994 and 1995, I'm not sure, at a patron saint's day in Dubica where there were quite a few people they said that they had taken their revenge on the Croats from that area for what happened in 1941.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local Serbs, who were at this gathering. That is what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So am I to understand from the way you've answered that question that you heard that from more than one person?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Several people talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear from any other source at any other time anything about what had happened at Dubica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it I think it was in around year 2000 when the ICTY made it known that crimes around Dubica were being investigated and that's when I heard from Savo Strbac that a mass crime committed against Croats in 1991 was under investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about what had happened there or did he just tell you that it was under investigation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that an investigation was underway but he told me more about his area, Benkovac, which he knew more about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I'll get to that in a moment. Let's talk now about the area of Korenica and Ogulin, specifically about Saborsko, Poljanak, and Lipovanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Your Honours, Korenica and Ogulin are visible on map 3 of the map book but it's also on page 19 of the atlas in the lower right part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us again which units were operating in this area during the fighting, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already mentioned that those were units from the training ground in Slunj. There was a command or rather parts of the Rijeka Corps. There was a special airborne unit from Nis. Then the 5th Partizan Brigade of the JNA, the Territorial Defence of Korenica municipality, and Plaski municipality. There were police units, and the base of the state security service had some units, I don't know which.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is that the state security service of the SAO Krajina or of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frenki's units, Frenki had its base there, Franko Simatovic from the State Security Service of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Saborsko, Poljanak, and Lipovanic, do you know if those were Croat villages, Serb villages, or mixed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Saborsko was a Croat village, and the other one was mostly Croat but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if there were Serb villages nearby?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know when there was fighting there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflicts there started on the 31st March 1991. There was a skirmish with the police which I talked about. However, the attack by the JNA began in end August, maybe early September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With respect to Saborsko, do you know specifically which units participated in the fighting in and around Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only that the 5th Partizan Brigade commanded by Cedo Bulat was involved in that northern area around Slunj and Plitvice lakes. I don't know any more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to pass through these villages at a later date, the ones we've just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1993, I passed through.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you see?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, villages that used to be populated by Croats and Croat houses were devastated and there were no Croat residents any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's talk now about Northern Dalmatia and specifically about Skabrnja, Nadin and Bruska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's at page 25 of the atlas, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Remind us again which units were operating there in that area.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Units of the 9th JNA Knin Corps were active there. Units of the TO from the area of Benkovac, and the units of the Krajina Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The units of the Krajina Police in that area, do you know who commanded them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special unit was commanded by Goran Opacic. The regular police was under the command of Drazic, I think. I think Drazic was the commander then. I'm not quite sure about that, about the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what the relationship was between Goran Opacic and Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Opacic was both subordinated to and close to Milan Martic. They were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was the president of the Benkovac municipality at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zdravko Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he have any relationship that you know of to Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991, until November, he was deputy president of the assembly of Krajina, but he was also part of the parallel government, together with Martic, and in February 1992, he became Prime Minister of the government of the Serbian Krajina, when I was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there a different kind of an organisational structure in Benkovac at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Benkovac had a peculiar structure, different from other parts of Krajina. They had a sort of Crisis Staff. It was called Crisis Staff of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was represented on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leadership of the Benkovac municipality, the police, and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit 124, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It has been shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a report from the Crisis Staff of the north, Dalmatia. It's the Crisis Staff of Zagreb, and that's a report that the government of Croatia had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So just to be clear because just a moment ago we were talking about the Crisis Staff of Benkovac, this is a different Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke earlier about the Serbian Crisis Staff in Benkovac, and this is the Croatian Crisis Staff from the same area, Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This document describes various events that occurred at that time. In the first paragraph it talks about mortar shells, second paragraph about an artillery attack, talks about private homes being targeted in the third paragraph, and so forth. Have you had an opportunity to read this entire document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is the report in this document about what happened in these areas accurate, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects faithfully the situation as it was in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 221, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit number 144, which is in evidence as Exhibit 40?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a report from the Krajina TO dated 16-17 September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could scroll down a little bit, it says there that "at 1750 hours, Secretary Milan Martic issued the following order." And then in point 2 there is a reference to the "armoured train." Is that the armoured train that you spoke about earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could scroll down a little bit further, just below point 4, it says, "At David Rastovic's request to organise the mopping up of Lovinac and Sveti Rok overnight using the Gracac forces." And it goes on. Can you remind us again who David Rastovic was at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the municipality of Donji Lapac was a member of this parallel government that I talked about, a close associate of Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it strange that in this report he's described as giving a request to mop up various areas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was involved in those fights, with Franko Simatovic and Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You described for us earlier remarks that Frenki Simatovic had about an attack on Lovinac. Is this related to that attack?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It happened after these events. I heard it from Simatovic after these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In October of 1991, did you have a conversation with General Vukovic of the 9th Corps relating to the area that included Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that conversation? How it came about and what occurred in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the signing of the agreement with representatives in Zadar, that is the agreement between the JNA command and the city of Zadar, about a cease-fire and the pullout of JNA units from Zadar, around that time, I was invited by General Vukovic to see him at his office, at the command of the 9th Corps in Knin. So I came, and he had in front of him a map of north Dalmatia, which was the area where the units of the 9th Corps of the JNA were deployed. He asked me to point out Serb-populated areas in that territory, Serb settlements. And he told me to pay special attention to the edge of that zone where his units were deployed. I enumerated all I knew and showed him all the Serb villages. He kept looking at the map and shaking his head, and then he said, "I can't wait for winter this way. I have to level it." He meant that he had to narrow down defence lines and regroup his forces and shorten the front line in order to have a better situation for the winter. That was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour I have just one last question on this topic and then it would be a convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What -- what did you understand him to mean that he had to shorten the front line and did this have any consequence for Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That area, especially the area of Benkovac and the environs of Zadar, was such that the contact line between Serb and Croat settlements was a curved line. I already explained how I understood Vukovic's comment, that he had to level it out and shorten the front line. If he deployed his units only across Serb settlements, he would get a very long line of deployment, and if he shortened it and made it a straight line, it would be a smaller area to defend, a shorter contact line with the opposite side. That's how I understood it. Of course, he didn't give me any details, but from what happened later on, I understood what happened. Skabrnja and Nagin [as interpreted] were deeper into the territory surrounded by Serbs and JNA and other forces, including the TO leveled that line in the military sense, and occupied the area of Skabrnja. Savo Strbac told me that expressly when I asked him why that had happened in Skabrnja and he said as much. He said they were deep into our territory and we had to take control. So my understanding of Vukovic's comment turned out to be correct. Of course, I couldn't know then what consequences that takeover would have and the consequences for the local population were terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I'll ask you some more questions about your conversation with Savo Strbac about this after the break but we are now overdue and I apologise for going over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourned. We will come back at quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic in the answer that you gave before the break, there was a reference as translated to us to Skabrnja and Nagin. Is it Nagin or Nadin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nadin. But I would like to say one more thing, if you allow me. Maybe I wasn't precise enough about the names of two people in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please do. Please explain.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning Drazic, I think he was for a while commander of the municipal TO Staff, whereas I had spoken earlier about the regular police. I wasn't sure. For a while, it was Vujko who commanded the regular police. That was perhaps the inaccuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Before the break, you started to tell us about a conversation that you had with Savo Srbac about what had happened at Skabrnja. When did you have that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That conversation was in year 2000, around that time, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did he tell you about Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that at the time, he headed the commission in charge of exchanging bodies of the dead between Benkovac and Zadar, that is between the Serb and Croat sides. He was on the Serb panel in Benkovac in charge of exchanging bodies. He spoke about events in Skabrnja because the Croat press reported it, and I don't know what the reports of the ICTY investigators were, but he commented on the press coverage. He said there had been no mass killings of civilians in Skabrnja and there had been no mass burials without marking the graves. He said that people were killed individually in fighting and everybody was buried in an individual grave that was marked, and the bodies were later delivered to the Croat side. That was his comment, and he also added that it wasn't true that Goran Opacic who was also known as Klempo had been involved in the fighting all the time. He said Goran Opacic had been there at the outset but later left. And that was his comment on those events, that I heard. And I did ask him, "Why did you do this over there? Why did this fighting occur at all?" And he said, "They were deep in our territory." And I said, "Who was involved?" And he answered, "Well, everybody, the police and the army."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you also have a conversation with him about what happened at Bruska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said Klempo, that is Goran Opacic, chief of the special police from Benkovac had thrown a hand grenade into a house in Bruska where there were Croats gathered and a Serb postman, killing everybody, and he said the man was mad. He said it was absolute madness, a folly, what he had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Savo Strbac have any connection to your making contact with the Office of the Prosecutor after you saw the Milosevic indictment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He put me in touch with the office of the Tribunal in Belgrade. In fact, he transmitted to them my message that I wanted contact with the Tribunal, and they informed the investigations here in The Hague, after which I got in touch with the investigators and the OTP. Even before that, he talked to me about cooperating with the Tribunal but concerning the investigation of the Croat Operation Storm in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that why he put you in touch with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, he is leading a non-governmental organisation that investigates crimes against Serbs committed by Croats, members of the Croat armed forces, in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you know if Savo Strbac made any statements concerning you at the time you pled guilty at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the moment when he put me in touch with the Tribunal, he was convinced that I would deny everything that was being said about me and about the Serbs in Krajina. After I started cooperating with the Tribunal, however, and after I testified in the Milosevic case, and especially after I pleaded guilty, he stated, before the press, that I used to be a firm man, and I had become a walkover, a rag.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, in the fall of 1991 or after, did you hear of any investigations or punishment of any Serbs in the SAO Krajina for having committed crimes during the war or during fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of 1991, I don't remember. Later on, there were investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you learn later on about investigations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one case in the area of Knin where members of the Serb army of the SAO Krajina had suffered some losses fighting with Croats and after that they killed Croat civilians in their own village, out of revenge, and then they were arrested either by the police or the military police and they were put in prison but I seem to have heard they had escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear about any other investigations for -- related to crimes committed against Croat civilians in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you spoke earlier in your testimony about prisons in Knin. Can you tell us, were there in the -- in the summer or fall of 1991, were there any prisoner exchanges between the Croat side and the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Prisoners and detainees, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police of the Krajina, or rather Mr. Martic, exchanged Croatian policemen that had been taken prisoners for Serb policemen who had been taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall any specific occasions when that occurred, that you could describe for us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I recall three situations that I was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Tell us about them, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember something that happened during the summer, perhaps it was the month of June, beginning of August, when the commander of the Knin Corps, General Nikovic, called me into his office and said to me that Martic has a prisoner from Sibenik, a policeman, and that he talked to representatives of the Sibenik police in terms of whether Martic could release him, and then he wanted the two of us to reach agreement. He said, "Let's you and me ask Martic together to release him." I think the policeman was released. But Mr. Martic, I guess, did not get any one in return in this exchange and then he said, in the newspapers later on, that he regretted having done it. That was one situation. Another situation was when I also received a message from some doctor from Zadar who is from the same area that I'm from, that Martic has a policeman who was taken prisoner and he asked me whether I could do something to have him set free. Then I called some of Martic's people, I think it was Amanovic, and asked whether they would release the man. They said they would. But since there was no exchange in return, then I would have to sign the document. I think that this man was also released. The third case was around the 10th or 12th of September 1991, during the visit of Ambassador Wijnaendts after the statement was signed in terms of accepting the European proposal on a cease-fire in Croatia. Ambassador Wijnaendts asked whether he could take some Croat prisoners along with him. I conveyed this information to Nikola Amanovic, Martic's assistant, to brought a list of prisoners that the Krajina Police held, and we handed this list over to Ambassador Wijnaendts who circled a group of people on this list that he took along with him. Those are the cases that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said with respect to the second case, the one -- when you received a message from a doctor in Zadar, that they told you that you would have to sign a document. Did you sign a document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter Exhibit 99, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, is this document, this one of 16-17 September 1991 in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, it isn't. Could it be put into evidence, please? Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see my notes and perhaps you're being told this as well by the Registrar, that it's already in evidence as Exhibit 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I apologise for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, thank you. I could very easily have missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, could we scroll down on the document, please? So we could read the text? Is -- do you recognise this document, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document that I was asked to sign in order to release the policeman from Zadar who was taken prisoner by the Krajina Police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, that document is not coming on my screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, aside from signing that document, did you do anything to release this person?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who released him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, did you hear anything during 1991 about how prisoners were treated in the prisons in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard towards the end of 1991, in the autumn, or at the end of 1991, from the justice minister in the Krajina government, Risto Matkovic that prisoners in jail were being mistreated by the police, who were detaining them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why did Risto Matkovic tell you that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said to me that we could, if I agree, have him talk to Mr. Martic, Minister of the Interior; if I agree, that he take measures and bring in professional prison guards so that this mistreatment would stop and that order would be imposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did it happen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1991. I cannot remember exactly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did somebody take charge of the prisons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professional prison guards, under the administration of Tauz. I think that was the name of the man who brought in this group of professional prison guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt? Why did Mr. Matkovic ask you if he may speak to Mr. Martic? Why didn't he just speak to Mr. Martic directly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Matkovic was Minister of Justice and administration in the government of the Krajina, and I was Prime Minister, so he was my minister for justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was Mr. Martic not his colleague in the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Martic was formally a colleague in the cabinet, but Martic for the most part did not honour decisions made by the government and his colleagues. Martic was only formally a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Had Martic been aware of this mistreatment of prisoners in jail before Mr. Matkovic spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He knew. He was the boss of those people who held the prison. It was his police that held the prison. He arrested people, imprisoned people, sent them to jail. Later on, I heard the citizens of Knin talking about this a great deal. So it was rather a -- well-known what was being done in that prison, that is. Martic's people were in charge of the prison. He had to know what went on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say Mr. Martic was just a formal member of the cabinet but of -- of the government and didn't cooperate with the government. Why, then, did he agree to the release of these prisoners after Mr. Matkovic had spoken to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that that was the time when negotiations started on engaging UN peacekeeping forces, and that that was the political moment when he became more amenable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But Mr. Martic would have been aware of these negotiations himself without Mr. Matkovic speaking to him, and he would have released them of his own volition if he wanted to use that as a chip in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say exactly what the reasons were, why he relented at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, with respect to Mr. Matkovic, after 1992, what did he do, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Matkovic became president Martic's adviser. For a while he was a judge and later on, because the assembly did not confirm him as a judge in Krajina, he became a member of President Martic's office and his adviser.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You spoke about Mr. Wijnaendts the ambassador, coming to the Krajina and that he -- you met with him and he had a list of prisoners which then you provided to Mr. Amanovic. First of all, Mr. Wijnaendts, do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you please repeat your question? I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Wijnaendts, the ambassador you spoke about, that came in September of 1991, the ambassador, do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've forgotten. Henry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He was an ambassador of which country, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an ambassador of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. He was the ambassador of the Netherlands to Paris but at that time the Netherlands was the presiding country or the coordinating country of the European Community. Van den Broek, the foreign minister, was superior to him, and I think that that is the reason why Mr. Henry Wijnaendts, the ambassador in Paris, became this coordinator or, rather in charge of a particular sector within the international conference on the former Yugoslavia that was being held in The Hague at that time, that autumn.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ambassador Wijnaendts, did you meet with him? You've already said you met with him. How many times did you meet with him in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of meeting with him? What was your purpose?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one had to agree to the accord made between the European Community and the representatives of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Croatia, on a cease-fire in the territory of Croatia, so that the conference that was being prepared could actually start, so that the peace talks could start on a final resolution to the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic meet with him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think so. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was this preparation for what was called later the Carrington plan? Did this lead up to the Carrington plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. We'll talk about that in a moment. I want to go back to the prisons. At that time, in the fall of 1991 -- I've been saying prisons. Was there one prison or was there more than one prison in Knin in the fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two prisons. One was held by the police of Krajina, and the other one was held by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the information that Mr. Matkovic gave you at the end of 1991 related to which prison, the JNA prison or the police prison?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if civilians were held in either of these prisons during 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that they were kept in the police prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 1995, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall who told you that or how you heard it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a relative of my wife, Jasminka, who told me that her mother who was a Croat was held in that prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified earlier in your testimony about Mr. Martic being arrested in Bosnia-Herzegovina in September of 1991 with Dusan Smiljanic. Now, I appreciate that you said in your answer earlier that you didn't know if he was arrested or detained or what the circumstances exactly were of him being held. Just for purposes of these questions I'll just the word arrest because it just is an easier word to use. What happened with him? How long was he held and how was he released, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened within a series of events that occurred between two visits paid by Ambassador Wijnaendts to Knin. That's how I know the date roughly, between the 8th and the 10th or 12th of September 1991. So this happened during the course of two or perhaps three days. There was one particular event that preceded Martic's detention in Otoka. Then the event that was related to his arrest or detention in Otoka and then his release from Otoka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the event that preceded the detention in Otoka of Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The event that preceded it caused a great deal of anxiety among the villagers of Otoka and Bosanska Krupa. This is the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they are ethnic Muslims, namely around the 8th of September, a group of Martic's men went through that village and they were being held there. It was also said that a journalist from Belgrade was being kept there. Then a group of their colleagues came and set them free. At any rate, at that time the population in Otoka was very upset. Mr. Martic was returning at the time from Kostajnica with Colonel or Major Smiljanic. I don't know what he was at that time. And the locals recognised him on the bridge on the Una, and they set up a blockade. The police took them to -- to the police station in Otoka and I think that the local people actually threw his car into the water. I'm not sure about that. What followed were events that I was involved in too, and that had to do with his release from Otoka. Or, rather, communications, talks, and finally getting Martic out of Otoka by a helicopter of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at intercept -- in the intercept bundle and if the witness could be provided with a bundle, and if we could look at intercept number 129 or that's the 65 ter number but that's how it's tabbed in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This time I didn't hear this document being put into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The order on Visi Kostman [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct, Your Honour. Could that be moved into evidence, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 222, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, have you found intercept number 129?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Maybe the usher could assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it. I found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just take a moment to look at that transcript, Mr. Babic? When you've had an opportunity to review it, could you just tell us generally what the conversation is about, as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation has to do with the first event in Otoka that I spoke of a few moments ago. That is to say, the event that preceded Martic's arrest in Otoka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, on the declaration and spreadsheet that was put into evidence, you identified -- you indicated or you said that you recognised the voices of Radovan Karadzic and Jovica Stanisic in this intercept. Can you tell us approximately how many times you have met face to face with Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About ten times perhaps, perhaps a bit more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you had occasion to speak with him on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to play any clips from this intercept. Could it be marked for identification, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The intercept is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification number 223, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look now at transcript number 131?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, in this conversation, you have identified and that -- your declaration that the participants in the conversation are Radovan Karadzic and yourself. Can you tell us what this conversation is about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was about what happened in Otoka, the second event that I've already spoken about. Martic's arrest. And his being held in Otoka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did this conversation occur as it has been transcribed and recorded? Did it in fact occur?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to play one clip from this conversation. It starts on the first page of the English and the first page also of the B/C/S, and it starts where Radovan Karadzic says, "Yes, then let them approach from the Novi Sad." From the top of the transcript it's indicated Radovan Karadzic is the second male voice and Milan Babic is the first voice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Radovan Karadzic is the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The second male voice is Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the witness is the first one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, if you could just listen to the transcript -- and I think we have to switch -- if the AV booth could switch us over to Sanction for this playing? I've gotten the nod. See if this works.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, in that little segment that we just heard, Radovan Karadzic says that Milosevic will inform Kadijevic and the army will get fully involved. What is that a reference to, as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The freeing of Martic from Otoka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He also says, "We'll bring this bloody mess with our partners to an end. We'll never forget what they did, and they will lose a state for what they have done tonight." How did you understand that statement from Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His partners were partners in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslims from the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move this intercept into evidence. Not marked for identification but into evidence. This is on a different footing than the other intercepts because Mr. Babic is a participant and he confirms that the conversation actually occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The intercept is -- intercept number 131 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 224, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
